thread_title: S. leucophylla var. alba-the chameleon effect
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla var. alba-the chameleon effect

posts.body_html:
"Mike Wang, you sent me this crap leuco clone and called it an alba, what gives?" While I've never heard anyone say that yet, it seems appropriate to pre-empt that conversation by posting these pictures. As a matter of fact, this will be a great post to reference to should such a conversation ever arise.

Not all leucophylla alba clones "interchange" between regular leucophylla and var. alba traps, but quite a few do. As a good example, take a look at this individual. Photos taken 8/4/16:


In this first picture, notice the two very different looking traps connect to the same exact plant(Edit: this clone is now called S. leucophylla var. alba 'original chameleon' Baldwin Co, AL):



perhaps this picture better shows the two traps connected to the same rhizome, the solid white one would be considered var. alba according to Stewy and Donnie Schnell, and the regular looking one would be merely called S. leucophylla....by Stewy and Donnie Schnell:




WTF? Same plant!



Closer pic, I would have never guessed this was an alba if that super white trap didn't pop out:



And just for fun, we've seen something similar with Hurricane creek white, but the less white pitchers still look more alba-ish than the clone referenced above: icps.proboards.com/thread/5595

posts.body_html:
Hi Bobby,

These can get to a meter tall under optimal conditions, but usually reach around 2-2.5' for me outdoors here in California. Other growers who baby these for Jesus can consistently produce 3' tall plants. I sometimes get very tall ones, but that's an exception to the rule. These are genetically different from the hurricane creek white cultivar: while hurricane creek whites do the chameleon thing, their "regular" looking traps are still whiter than non-albas . With some of these other clones that I have, the phenotypic variance is so extreme, you sometimes can't even tell it's an alba until the late summer/early fall pitchers show up.

Here's another confirmed "Chameleon" leucophylla var. alba. I don't remember where I read this, but someone was commenting how there's a lot of leucophyllas eroneously mislabeled as albas. They were likely looking at plants that I labeled as albas that have the "chameleon effect." Not too many people have read this post, but it'll be common knowledge in the near future that some genotypes of S. leucophylla var. alba have extreme phenotypic variances to the point that they aren't recognizable as albas until certain specific environmental conditions are met.

Had you not seen the photos above, you'd probably say I'm not being truthful that the plant below is a verified S. leucophylla var. alba, but this plant produced solid, snow white traps last year! Photos taken 4/20/17:

posts.body_html:
Nat: I heard that gangsta rap keeps these plants strong and on their feet, especially when they listen to NWA (north west alatas)....

With regards to color, I think the factors that affect it are dynamic, but I don't truly know yet. Rob S. informed me he cuts all the traps off down to the ground on his rubricorpora plants during the winter and they're solid red with yellow tops when new growth resumes the next season. When I do the same thing, all of my plants turn mostly green throughout the grow season.

Leucophyllas are different beasts compared to S. flava var. rubricorpora because they have all season long to do their thing before fall traps are produced. Last winter (2015-2016) I cut off all the traps to the ground on my hurricane creek white bed and in the fall of 2016, it was the best, whitest, and most dense trap production that I've ever seen:


Perhaps light and temperature play a pretty darn big role in pigment coloration, but one thing I also want to investigate is how does the type of prey being consumed affect trap coloration? I think what they catch in the spring and summer might have a big effect on coloration since this is the primary source of nutrition stored into the rhizome and then consumed for the fall pitcher show.

Another thing we don't tend to pay attention to is rate of growth of the fall traps. I wonder if slower growth rates produce more intense colors? No idea....
